Guides

When your child is ill

Familiar food, enough fluids, and the usual milk feeds. A sick day is the wrong day to decide on an allergy or try a new food.

Key points

Fluids and milk come before a perfect menu. Small, familiar meals are enough. Don’t make a young child go without food.
Don’t introduce a new allergen while your child is ill. You can’t tell what a rash or vomiting means on that day.
Know the signs that need a doctor the same day. Few wet nappies, a sunken soft spot (fontanelle), blood in the stool, unusual sleepiness, or laboured breathing are not things to watch and wait on at home.

Feeding a poorly child

Fever and a sore mouth both dampen appetite. Keep up breast milk or formula. Offer smaller amounts of foods your child already likes: yogurt, fruit, plain porridge, or unsalted broth is enough. Pushing a balanced plate on a child who feels sick can put them off food.

If your child is vomiting or has diarrhoea and milk alone isn’t keeping up, oral rehydration solution is the right tool. Your health visitor can talk you through it. Sugary juice is a poor substitute and can make diarrhoea worse.

Save new foods for a healthy week

Illness changes skin and stools. A new food on the same day can create a false allergy story, and a food the family then avoids for years. Wait until your child is well, then pick up the introduction plan again.

Teething and illness often get blamed for each other. More than a slight temperature, or a child who is clearly unwell, can’t be put down to a tooth. Get them checked.

When to call a doctor

Call the same day if your child is under three months old and has a fever, is unusually floppy or hard to wake, is struggling to breathe, has blood in their vomit or stool, or isn’t passing urine. In these situations, food advice doesn’t matter.

After antibiotics, there’s no need for a special ‘cleanse’. Ordinary food is fine, including yogurt if they like it. Probiotics are optional, not a necessary part of recovery.
